parole.significato: affix appended in declension of мати (maty, “mother”)
hump, knoll, dune (A small gentle hill)
parole.testo: Related to Russian кочегур (kočegur), Russian кочка (kočka), Serbo-Croatian kočegura, from Proto-Balto-Slavic, whence Latvian cekuls, Latvian cecers, Lithuanian kẽkulas. From Proto-Indo-European *kek- or *kok-, whence also Albanian qikël.

parole.significato: to tie a rope on the horns of a cow/ox/etc.

parole.testo: From older прозвисько (prozvysʹko), from Old East Slavic прозъв (prozŭv). Related to звати (zvaty, “to call”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewH- (“to call, invoke”). By surface analysis, прізвище (prizvyšče) + -исько (-ysʹko).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian та́нути (tánuti), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂- + *-nǫti.
By surface analysis, у- (u-) + спі́ти (spíty), from Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“press, hurry”), whence English speed. Cognate with Russian успе́ть (uspétʹ).

Melnychuk posits inheritance from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keu-l- (“to cut”), related to *(s)keu-r (whence щу́рити (ščúryty)). Compare Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut; to split, to separate”) and *(s)ker- (“to cut off, sever; to separate, divide”), Russian щу́рить (ščúritʹ).

Compare Polish zupa, Latvian zupa, Yiddish זופּ (zup). Likely from the Polish, which is itself from German Suppe, from Old French souppe, sope. Per ESSJa, inherited from Proto-Slavic *mitь, related to Proto-Slavic *mitě, *mitъ, *mimo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“change”). Alternatively, from earlier меть (metʹ, “throw, sweep, motion”), from мета́ти (metáty).

parole.significato: station (e.g. in transportation, or as part of a supply network)
parole.testo: Either from Polish stacja with contamination from стан (stan), or else borrowed from Polish stancja (“lodgings”) with subsequent conflation with Polish stacja. All sources ultimately derive from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.
